guided.title: Employees with a heavy order
guided.prompt: Return `employee_id` and `last_name` of the employees who have handled at least one order with `freight` above 150. Use `EXISTS` with a correlated subquery on `orders`, so each employee appears once. Order by `employee_id`.
guided.starter:
-- Employees who handled at least one order with freight above 150
SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name
FROM employees e
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name
FROM employees e
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM orders o
              WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id
                AND o.freight > 150)
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
hints: The starter lists every employee. Add a WHERE clause that asks whether a matching heavy order exists.
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE ...) with the correlation o.employee_id = e.employee_id.
Add AND o.freight > 150 inside the subquery.

guided.title: German customers who never bought an expensive line
guided.prompt: Return `customer_id` of the customers in Germany who have no order line with a line price above 50 (`order_details.unit_price > 50`). The subquery joins `orders` to `order_details`. Use `NOT EXISTS`. Order by `customer_id`.
guided.starter:
-- German customers with no order line priced above 50
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'Germany'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM orders o
                  JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                    AND od.unit_price > 50)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
hints: The starter returns all German customers. The extra condition says that something does not exist.
NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_details od ON ... WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND ...).
Inside the subquery add od.unit_price > 50 and join od.order_id = o.order_id.

guided.title: Fix the NOT IN trap
guided.prompt: Return `employee_id` and `last_name` of the employees who have no orders at all. The starter uses `NOT IN` and returns nothing, because one order has a NULL `employee_id`. Rewrite it with `NOT EXISTS`. Order by `employee_id`.
guided.starter:
-- Employees with no orders (the NOT IN version returns nothing)
SELECT employee_id, last_name
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM orders)
ORDER BY employee_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id)
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
hints: Run the starter: it returns no rows, because the list produced by the subquery contains a NULL.
NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery does not mind NULL values in the other table.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id)

guided.title: Count customers, not rows
guided.prompt: Return one row with the column `customers`: the number of customers who have at least one order whose `ship_country` is Germany. The starter joins and counts rows, so customers with several such orders are counted several times. Use `EXISTS`.
guided.starter:
-- Number of customers with at least one order shipped to Germany
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.ship_country = 'Germany';
guided.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.ship_country = 'Germany');
hints: Run the starter and compare its number with the number of different customers: a join returns one row per order.
Test the customer row, not the pairs: keep customers for which a matching order exists.
FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.ship_country = 'Germany')

independent.title: Customers who arrived in 1997 and stayed
independent.prompt: Return `customer_id` and `company_name` of the customers who placed at least one order in 1997 (from 1997-01-01 up to but not including 1998-01-01), at least one order from 1998-01-01 on, and no order before 1997-01-01. Use `EXISTS` and `NOT EXISTS`. Order by `customer_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Customers with orders in 1997 and 1998 and none before 1997
SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date >= '1998-01-01')
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.order_date >= '1997-01-01' AND o.order_date < '1998-01-01')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date >= '1998-01-01')
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date < '1997-01-01')
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

independent.title: Employees who never shipped late
independent.prompt: Return `employee_id` and `last_name` of the employees who have at least one order but none shipped late (`shipped_date` after `required_date`). Use one `EXISTS` and one `NOT EXISTS`. Order by `employee_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Employees with orders, none of them shipped late
SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id AND o.shipped_date > o.required_date)
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name
FROM employees e
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id
                    AND o.shipped_date > o.required_date)
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

independent.title: Products bought in both Germany and France
independent.prompt: Stretch task. Return `product_id` and `product_name` of the products that appear in order lines of orders placed by a customer in Germany and also in order lines of orders placed by a customer in France (use the customer's `country`). Use two `EXISTS` conditions, each with a subquery joining `order_details`, `orders` and `customers`. Order by `product_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Products ordered by customers in Germany and also by customers in France
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_details od
              JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = od.order_id
              JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
              WHERE od.product_id = p.product_id AND c.country = 'Germany')
ORDER BY p.product_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_details od
              JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = od.order_id
              JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
              WHERE od.product_id = p.product_id AND c.country = 'Germany')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_details od
              JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = od.order_id
              JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
              WHERE od.product_id = p.product_id AND c.country = 'France')
ORDER BY p.product_id;

checks.question: One order (10347) in `orders` has a NULL `employee_id`. What does `SELECT ... FROM employees WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM orders)` return when employee 5 has no orders?
options: Employee 5 only
All employees except those with orders, which includes employee 5
No rows, because the NULL in the list makes NOT IN never true
An error because of the NULL
checks.explanation: x NOT IN (..., NULL) expands to x <> a AND x <> b AND ... AND x <> NULL. The last comparison is unknown, so the whole condition is never true and WHERE keeps nothing. NOT EXISTS has no such problem and returns employee 5.

checks.question: What does `SELECT customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders)` (without a correlation) return?
options: Customers with orders
Every customer, because the subquery returns rows regardless of the customer
No customers
An error, since the subquery is not correlated
checks.explanation: Without the correlation o.customer_id = c.customer_id, the subquery returns rows for every outer row, so EXISTS is true for all of them. The query is valid but not what you meant.

checks.question: Customer BONAP has two orders dated 1998. How many times does BONAP appear in `customers c JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE o.order_date >= '1998-01-01'`, and how many in the `EXISTS` version?
options: Twice and twice
Once and once
Twice and once
Once and twice
checks.explanation: A join returns one row per matching order, so BONAP appears twice. EXISTS tests the customer row and returns it once. That is why a semi-join is safer when you count customers.

checks.question: What does the select list of the subquery in `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE ...)` do?
options: It decides which column is compared
Nothing important: EXISTS only checks whether any row is returned
It must match a column of the outer query
It is returned to the outer query
checks.explanation: EXISTS tests for the presence of a row. SELECT 1, SELECT * or SELECT NULL all behave the same. By convention SELECT 1 shows that the values do not matter.

checks.question: Which of these is a NULL-safe way to list customers without any order?
options: WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
WHERE customer_id <> ALL (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
WHERE customer_id <> (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
checks.explanation: NOT EXISTS ignores NULL values in the other table. NOT IN and <> ALL have the same NULL trap, and the last form fails when the subquery returns more than one row.

checks.question: Which expression combines two existence questions: customers with an order in 1998 and no order in 1996?
options: EXISTS (...1998...) OR NOT EXISTS (...1996...)
EXISTS (...1998...) AND NOT EXISTS (...1996...)
NOT EXISTS (...1998...) AND EXISTS (...1996...)
checks.explanation: Both conditions must hold, so they are joined with AND: one EXISTS for 1998 and one NOT EXISTS for 1996. OR would accept customers satisfying either condition, and the last option is the reverse question.
